competitors.name: TariffRefund
competitors.what_they_do: Self-serve guided platform that helps US importers of record calculate, prepare and file IEEPA refund claims with CBP. Positions itself against customs brokers and consultants. Importer-side only. The site does not mention downstream buyers, surcharge pass-through or claims against suppliers.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Waitlist and early access from April 20, 2026. Flat fee with no percentage of refunds. No team or funding disclosed on the site. Claims SOC 2 compliance.

competitors.name: PRGX (recovery audit / AP profit recovery)
competitors.what_they_do: Long-established recovery-audit firm that mines client AP and payment data for overpayments and recovers them from suppliers. Also does contract compliance and retail profit recovery. The homepage does not mention tariffs or contingency fees. Its core competency is nearly identical to this idea's workflow (mine invoices, claim from suppliers, track to closure) and it could add a tariff-surcharge module quickly.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Claims clients in 30+ countries and $1.8B in annual cash flow recovered. Established, PE-owned company (ownership not verified this session).

competitors.name: Cass Information Systems (freight audit and payment)
competitors.what_they_do: Freight and transportation invoice validation, audit and payment for shippers. This is the incumbent category for the idea's second module (fuel and freight surcharge auditing). The homepage does not specify fuel-surcharge audit or tariff features.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Public company with a large installed base of shippers.

competitors.name: AFS Logistics (freight audit, parcel audit, post-audit)
competitors.what_they_do: Parcel, freight, ocean and post-audit services to find invoice errors, plus tariff-uncertainty advisory through forwarding. Also occupies the fuel-surcharge audit space.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Established 3PL and freight audit vendor. Funding not checked.

competitors.name: Other freight-audit vendors (nVision Global, Trax Technologies)
competitors.what_they_do: Freight audit and payment providers that would cover the fuel-surcharge audit module. The site fetches returned little or no content (Trax returned 503), so their offerings are unverified.

white_space: Provisional: I found no product or startup that mines a buyer's supplier invoices for tariff surcharge lines and pursues the supplier for a share of the IEEPA refund, on the buyer's behalf and for a contingency fee. The importer side is being served (TariffRefund.com self-serve, plus customs brokers and consultants). Freight and parcel audit vendors cover surcharge auditing. Generic AP recovery audit (PRGX) is the closest capability. What looks unserved is the buyer-as-claimant workflow: an automated surcharge ledger, supplier IEEPA-exposure estimates, contract pass-back language checks, claim letters, and CBP Form 4811 notify-party routing. It would target mid-market multi-unit franchisees, buying co-ops and GPOs, who are too small for PRGX-style enterprise engagements. The fuel-surcharge module is NOT white space because freight audit is a mature, crowded category. Caveat: my competitor scan is incomplete. The web-search budget was exhausted before any search ran, so this rests on direct page fetches of the CBP page, earnings transcripts and a handful of guessed vendor sites. Law-firm class actions or demand-letter campaigns, tariff-refund startups I could not surface, and customs brokers or couriers adding a pass-through service were not checked.
evidence_of_demand: Mixed. The underlying money and the pass-through gap are verified, but I found no direct evidence that downstream buyers are paying for a clawback service. (1) The refund flows only to the importer of record or its designated 4811 party, and CBP says nothing about downstream buyers: https://www.cbp.gov/trade/programs-administration/trade-remedies/ieepa-duty-refunds. (2) Windfalls are large and are being kept. AutoZone booked $96M in IEEPA refunds, and its CFO said the refund environment was deflationary, i.e. cost relief to retailers and suppliers rather than customer credits: https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/22/autozone-azo-q4-2026-earnings-call-transcript/. Cracker Barrel booked $15M ($9.1M net after reinvestment), with no mention of suppliers or pass-through: https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/23/cracker-barrel-cbrl-q4-2026-earnings-call-transcript/. MillerKnoll booked $16.5M (180 bps of gross margin), did not address refunds of customer surcharges, and announced a new 4% pricing action: https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/22/mlkn-q1-2027-earnings-call-transcript/. (3) Willingness to pay for importer-side help is shown by TariffRefund.com, which claims 330,000+ eligible importers with an average refund of about $503K (self-reported marketing): https://www.tariffrefund.com/. (4) Willingness to pay contingency-style recovery audits on supplier invoices is shown by PRGX's claimed $1.8B in annual recoveries: https://www.prgx.com. (5) Not found: forum complaints from buyers, RFPs, or buyer-side customers of any clawback service. Legal entitlement is also unproven, since a buyer who paid a price or surcharge often has no contractual right to the supplier's refund.
sharper_angle: Narrow to the claims that have a real legal hook and a buyer with leverage, and drop the fuel-surcharge module, which is a crowded freight-audit category. (1) Sell to buying groups, franchisee co-ops, GPOs and distribution co-ops as one negotiated, portfolio-level claim, not to individual franchisees. Leverage is collective, and their supply agreements often carry cost-plus, most-favored-customer, pass-through or 'refund if rescinded' clauses. (2) Screen every claim up front for an itemized tariff line or explicit pass-back language, and drive only those, jointly with a trade or commercial-litigation firm. The firm carries the legal risk and the product supplies the evidence: a clean surcharge ledger plus each supplier's estimated IEEPA exposure. This also makes the product a feed for plaintiffs' firms, which is a likelier revenue path than solo recovery. (3) Consider a supplier-side variant: a workflow that lets importers route refunds or credit memos to customers via 4811 and documents it. Large buyers will demand this in procurement, and suppliers want to keep goodwill without a dispute. (4) Move fast, because the window is roughly Q3-Q4 2026 and PRGX-type recovery-audit firms or TariffRefund.com could add a downstream module. Before building, re-run the competitor scan with working web search (tariff-refund pass-through startups, YC and Product Hunt, class actions and law-firm demand-letter campaigns, and customs brokers and couriers) and get a trade lawyer's view on whether buyers have any enforceable claim.
